newsitem.title: USA: Nader study opposes Staples-Office Depot merger.
newsitem.headline: Nader study opposes Staples-Office Depot merger.

text.p: Consumer advocate Ralph Nader released a study Monday that found lower prices where Staples Inc. and Office Depot Inc. stores compete with each other and called on the government to prevent their merger.

Staples and Office Depot have been running full-page ads in major newspapers promising to lower prices if their proposed $3.5 billion merger wins government approval, but Nader said his study showed the opposite was likely to occur.
The Federal Trade Commission, considering whether to allow the merger under antitrust laws, earlier delayed a final decision until next week and requested more information, the companies said.

Nader and his colleagues said their study, conducted Feb. 20-21 at 15 randomly selected Staples and 17 randomly selected Office Depot stores, showed prices on house brand fax paper were cheaper where the stores competed.
They said the merger was a bad deal for consumers.

"Office Depot told us that the price for this item was uniform throughout the country, but in the 17 Office Depot locations surveyed we found six different prices, ranging from $19.99 to $27.99, a difference of 40 percent," the study said.
At Staples, the survey found prices ranging from $13.99 to $27.99, "a difference of 97 percent," the survey said.

"Competition between Staples and Office Depot (is) particularly important in lowering prices," Nader and his colleagues at the Consumer Project on Technology of the Centre for Study of Responsive Law wrote.
"These data are evidence that the proposed merger will result in higher prices and harm consumers," the study said.

Staples' director of investor relations, Sam Levenson, said from company headquarters in Westborough, Mass., that he needed to "see the survey and find out if it is statistically relevant" before he could comment.
After it was provided, a secretary said Levenson and other officials were in a meeting and would be unavailable for the rest of the day.
In an interview, Nader said the study was one of the clearest cases he had ever seen of the effect of competition.
"The irony is they're spending tens of thousands of dollars on advertisements saying they want to merge in order to reduce their gross sales," Nader said.
In a letter to the FTC, the Nader group said its study cast a new light on the proposal.

"We believe the Staples/Office Depot Merger ... is illegal under the Clayton Act," wrote Nader, James Love and Robert Wiesman. "As consumers of both Office Depot and Staples, we urge the commission to reject the merger." The Clayton Act is the nation's premier antitrust law.
In their letter, Nader and his colleagues also asked to meet with the FTC to present their data.
A spokeswoman for the Federal Trade Commission declined to comment.
